public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 466

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/466](https://www.erdosproblems.com/466)
- [Er72] Erdős, Paul, *Extremal problems in number theory*. Proceedings of the 1972 Number Theory
  Conference (Univ. Colorado, Boulder, Colo.) (1972), 80-86.
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
- [Er82e] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favourite problems which recently have been solved*. (1982),
  59-79.
- [Sa76] Sárközy, A., *On distances near integers. I, II*. Studia Sci. Math. Hungar. (1976), 37-50,
  105-111.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter Metric

namespace Erdos466

/--
`N X δ` is the maximum number of points in a closed disc of radius `X` in the plane such that
the distance between any two of them is at least `δ` away from the nearest integer.
-/
noncomputable def N (X δ : ℝ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {n | ∃ (c : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)) (P : Finset (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))),
    P.card = n ∧ ↑P ⊆ closedBall c X ∧
      (P : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))).Pairwise fun x y => δ ≤ distToNearestInt (dist x y)}

/--
Let $N(X,\delta)$ denote the maximum number of points $P_1,\ldots,P_n$ which can be chosen in a
circle of radius $X$ such that
$$\| \lvert P_i-P_j\rvert \| \geq \delta$$
for all $1\leq i<j\leq n$. (Here $\|x\|$ is the distance from $x$ to the nearest integer.)

Is there some $\delta>0$ such that
$$\lim_{X\to \infty}N(X,\delta)=\infty?$$

Graham proved this is true, and in fact $N(X,1/10)> \frac{\log X}{10}$. This was substantially
improved by Sárközy [Sa76], who proved that for all sufficiently small $\delta>0$,
$N(X,\delta)>X^{1/2-\delta^{1/7}}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 52, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos466.lean#L292"]
theorem erdos_466 : answer(True) ↔ ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ Tendsto (fun X ↦ N X δ) atTop atTop := by
  sorry

/-- Graham proved that $N(X,1/10)> \frac{\log X}{10}$. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 52]
theorem erdos_466.variants.graham : ∀ X : ℝ, 1 ≤ X → Real.log X / 10 < N X (1 / 10) := by
  sorry

/--
Sárközy [Sa76] proved that for all sufficiently small $\delta>0$,
$N(X,\delta)>X^{1/2-\delta^{1/7}}$ for all sufficiently large $X$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 52]
theorem erdos_466.variants.sarkozy : ∃ δ₀ : ℝ, 0 < δ₀ ∧ ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → δ < δ₀ →
    ∀ᶠ X : ℝ in atTop, X ^ (1 / 2 - δ ^ (1 / 7 : ℝ)) < N X δ := by
  sorry

end Erdos466

reformulations.difference: The source's 'maximum number of points which can be chosen in a circle of radius X' is formalized as an sSup over ℕ of the sizes of finite point sets in a closed disc of radius X with an arbitrary centre. For δ ≤ 0 and X > 0 the set of sizes is unbounded, so the sSup is the default value 0 rather than a maximum.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For δ > 0, distToNearestInt d ≤ d for d ≥ 0, so admissible sets are δ-separated inside a compact disc. The set of sizes is therefore bounded and nonempty, and the sSup equals the genuine maximum. I proved the boundedness in Lean (S_bddAbove, via a finite δ/3-net), and also showed that the junk value N X δ = 0 occurs for δ ≤ 0. Every statement in the file evaluates N only at δ > 0: 0 < δ in erdos_466, δ = 1/10 in graham, 0 < δ in sarkozy. A disc of any centre is equivalent to a centred one by translation invariance. 'In a circle' means 'in a disc', as in Er72 (|z_i| ≤ n) and Goenka–Moore (closed ball). Closed versus open disc does not affect any of the statements.

reformulations.difference: The source states Graham's bound N(X,1/10) > log X/10 without saying for which X. The Lean statement claims it for every real X ≥ 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: I proved the Lean statement exactly as written, from the file's own definitions and without sorry (checked with type_of% against the declaration). The proof uses Graham's points (2^m, 4^m): m points fit in radius 2·4^m and all pairwise distances are more than 1/10 from an integer. For X ≥ 1 with log X < 10, a single point already gives N ≥ 1 > log X/10. Otherwise m = ⌊log X/10⌋+1 satisfies 2·4^m ≤ X. So the added range does not make the claim false, and it implies the 'for all large X' reading.

reformulations.difference: The source says 'for all sufficiently small δ>0, N(X,δ) > X^{1/2−δ^{1/7}}' and leaves the quantifier over X implicit. The Lean statement makes it explicit as ∀ᶠ X in atTop, after ∃ δ₀ > 0, ∀ δ ∈ (0, δ₀).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The bound is asymptotic in X. Er82e states Sárközy's result as: for every ε>0 there is δ(ε)>0 such that for every δ<δ(ε), N(x,δ) > x^{1/2−ε}, for large x. Goenka–Moore state it as N_2(X,δ) = Ω_δ(X^{1/2−ε}) as X → ∞, and their 3D analogue has the form 'for all X ≥ X_0(δ)'. So 'eventually in X, with a threshold depending on δ' is the intended reading, and the docstring says so explicitly. The exponent elaborates over ℝ as (1/2 : ℝ) − δ^(1/7 : ℝ), so there is no ℕ-division trap.

could_not_verify: Erdos466.erdos_466.variants.sarkozy — I could not check the exact form of Sárközy's theorem (exponent 1/2 − δ^{1/7}, no extra constant) against [Sa76] itself. Studia Sci. Math. Hungar. 11 (1976) has no accessible online copy and zbMATH has no review. The Lean statement and docstring match erdosproblems.com's LaTeX word for word. Er82e gives the weaker ε-form, which the δ^{1/7} form implies. My own rebuild of a Sárközy-type digit construction (points (Σα_i k^i, Σα_i k^{2i+1}), checked numerically) loses only about δ^{1/3}/log(1/δ) in the exponent. So the statement as written looks true, and its research-solved tag is not attached to a false claim.
review.notes:
No findings and no status issues. The source (erdosproblems.com/466, 'PROVED – solved in the affirmative'; teorth problems.yaml 'proved') agrees with `research solved`, `answer(True)` and the formal_proof link. The link points at the proved theorem (line 292), which uses an equivalent definition of N.

Lean checks in /workspace/review/port*.lean, all sorry-free, all using the file's own definitions:
(1) For δ > 0 the set in N is bounded above, so N is a genuine maximum.
(2) The exact type of `Erdos466.erdos_466`, i.e. True ↔ ∃ δ>0, N(·,δ) → ∞, is provable via Graham's (2^m, 4^m) construction. It holds through a real construction, not a default value.
(3) The exact type of `Erdos466.erdos_466.variants.graham` (∀ X ≥ 1) is provable.
(4) The default value N X δ = 0 when δ ≤ 0 and X > 0 exists, but no statement reaches it.

Minor, not reported as findings: the [Sa76] page range '105-111' is copied from erdosproblems.com, while zbMATH gives 105–112. The erdosproblems LaTeX has a lowercase 'lim_{x→∞}' typo, which the docstring correctly writes as X→∞.
